title: Mental Health Awareness
summary: Understand mental health and common conditions, challenge stigma, support someone who is struggling, respond safely in a crisis and look after your own wellbeing. An awareness course, not clinical training.
audience: Students, teachers, managers, parents, community leaders and anyone who wants to support others

body.p: Mental health is a state of wellbeing in which people can cope with the normal stresses of life, learn and work well, and contribute to their community. It is not simply the absence of illness: everyone has mental health, which can move between thriving, struggling and being unwell, just like physical health.

body.h: How common are mental health conditions?

body.p: The World Health Organization estimated that about 1 in 8 people worldwide were living with a mental disorder in 2019. In a class of 40 students, that would be about 5 people; in a workplace of 1000, about 125. Anxiety and depression are the most common. Most people recover or manage their condition well with the right support.

list: Biological factors: genetics, physical illness, substance use.
Psychological factors: coping skills, past experiences, including trauma.
Social factors: poverty, unemployment, discrimination, conflict, isolation and family stress.
Protective factors: supportive relationships, safe communities, meaningful activity, physical activity, sleep and access to care.

body.tip: This course builds awareness and basic support skills. It does not train you to diagnose or treat; that is the role of qualified health professionals.

body.p: Knowing the signs helps people seek help earlier. Only qualified professionals can diagnose, but anyone can notice changes and offer support.

list: Depression: persistent low mood or loss of interest for most days over at least two weeks, with changes in sleep, appetite, energy and concentration, and feelings of worthlessness.
Anxiety disorders: excessive worry or fear that is hard to control, with physical symptoms such as a racing heart, restlessness or panic attacks, and avoidance of situations.
Post-traumatic stress: after a frightening event, distressing memories or nightmares, avoidance, feeling on edge and changes in mood.
Psychosis: losing touch with reality, such as hearing voices others cannot hear or holding unusual fixed beliefs; needs prompt medical assessment.
Substance use problems: using alcohol or drugs in ways that cause harm, with loss of control and difficulty stopping.
Bipolar disorder: periods of depression and periods of unusually high mood and energy (mania).

body.p: Children and adolescents may show distress differently, through irritability, behaviour changes, falling school performance or physical complaints.

body.tip: Look for changes from a person's usual self that last weeks and affect daily life, rather than a single bad day.

body.p: Stigma means negative attitudes and discrimination towards people with mental health conditions. It stops people seeking help, harms relationships and employment, and can lead to human-rights abuses.

list: Use respectful, person-first language: "a person living with depression", not "a depressive" or insulting words.
Challenge myths: mental illness is not a personal weakness, a lack of faith or something people choose.
Share accurate information and stories of recovery.
Treat mental and physical health as equally important.

body.p: Communities explain distress in different ways, and many people first turn to family, faith leaders or traditional healers. Respecting beliefs while encouraging access to evidence-based care works better than dismissing them. Many countries are expanding mental health care in primary clinics and communities, sometimes using trained lay counsellors and talking therapies.

body.tip: If someone tells you about their mental health, thank them for trusting you; how you respond shapes whether they seek help again.

body.p: You do not need to be an expert to help. Early, kind support can make a big difference.

steps: Approach privately and gently: "I've noticed you seem low lately. How are you doing?"
Listen without judging or rushing to fix things; let them talk.
Give hope and accurate information: these problems are common and treatable.
Encourage professional help: a clinic, doctor, counsellor or psychologist; offer to help them make the first contact.
Encourage self-help and other supports: trusted people, routines, sleep, activity, and avoiding alcohol and drugs.
Follow up and stay in touch.

list: Telling people to "snap out of it" or "be grateful".
Gossiping or sharing their story without permission, unless safety requires it.
Promising to keep a secret if their safety or someone else's is at risk.

body.tip: Look after yourself too; supporting someone can be draining, so share the load with others and seek support for yourself.

body.p: Sometimes a person is in immediate danger: they may talk about wanting to die, be extremely distressed, confused or aggressive, or have taken a harmful substance. Stay calm and focus on safety.

body.h: If someone may be thinking about suicide

list: Take it seriously, every time.
Ask directly and calmly whether they are thinking about suicide. Research shows that asking does not put the idea into someone's head; it often brings relief.
Listen and stay with them, or make sure someone safe stays with them.
Help them connect with urgent help: a crisis line, a health facility or emergency services.
If there is immediate danger, call your local emergency number.

body.p: Find out now which crisis lines and emergency services operate in your country and save the numbers in your phone. Many countries have free helplines run by health services or NGOs, such as SADAG in South Africa.

For panic attacks, help the person to a quieter place, speak calmly and encourage slow breathing. For someone who seems confused, seeing or hearing things others do not, or who may harm others, keep yourself and others safe and seek medical or emergency help.

body.tip: If you are struggling yourself, please reach out to someone you trust or a local helpline. You do not have to cope alone.

body.p: Everyone can take steps to protect their mental health. No single habit is a cure, but together they build resilience.

list: Connect: spend time with people who support you.
Move: regular physical activity improves mood and sleep.
Sleep: keep regular sleep times and limit screens before bed.
Learn and do meaningful activities: hobbies, volunteering, faith or cultural activities.
Notice your thoughts and feelings; practices such as mindfulness, prayer or journalling help some people.
Limit alcohol and avoid drugs, which worsen anxiety and depression.
Ask for help early when things feel too much.

body.p: Organisations can support mental health through reasonable workloads, clear roles, anti-bullying policies, training managers and teachers to notice distress, flexible arrangements, confidential counselling services and reasonable adjustments for people with mental health conditions. Supportive environments improve wellbeing, attendance and performance.

body.tip: Pick one small habit, such as a daily walk or a regular bedtime, and keep it for two weeks before adding another.

quiz.q: Mental health is best described as:
options: A state of wellbeing that everyone has and that can change over time

quiz.q: WHO estimated that in 2019 about how many people lived with a mental disorder?
Using that estimate, about how many people in a class of 40?
Which is a sign of depression?
options: Persistent low mood and loss of interest for at least two weeks

quiz.q: Hearing voices others cannot hear may be a sign of:
Which phrase is respectful, person-first language?

options: Negative attitudes and discrimination towards people with mental health conditions

quiz.q: When supporting someone, you should first:
options: Tell them to snap out of it

quiz.q: If a friend asks you to keep a secret but their safety is at risk, you should:
options: Not promise secrecy and get help
Keep it secret no matter what

quiz.q: Does asking someone directly about suicide increase their risk?
options: Only if asked by a stranger
No, it often brings relief and opens the door to help

quiz.q: If someone is in immediate danger, you should:
options: Leave them alone to calm down
Stay with them and call emergency services or a crisis line

quiz.q: How can workplaces support mental health?
Who can diagnose a mental health condition?
